name: Retail
one_liner: Businesses that buy goods from manufacturers and resell them to consumers through stores and digital channels, with economics defined by thin margins, inventory turns, and store productivity.
how_it_makes_money: Retailers earn the spread between purchase cost and selling price, and scale players supplement it with vendor funding, membership fees, private-label margin, and increasingly retail media advertising. Profitability depends on turning inventory quickly and spreading fixed store and supply-chain costs over high volume.
revenue_formula: Revenue = number of stores × sales per store (traffic × conversion × average basket)
Same-store sales growth = traffic change + ticket change
Revenue = customers × visits per year × spend per visit (plus membership or ad income)
cost_structure: Cost of goods sold: by far the largest cost, often roughly 60-75% of sales depending on format
Store labor: the largest operating expense and a key target of scheduling and automation
Occupancy: rent, utilities, and maintenance of the store fleet
Supply chain and fulfillment: DCs, trucking, and last-mile costs for online orders
Shrink and markdowns: theft, damage, and clearance of unsold inventory
margins: Operating margins are thin, roughly 2-5% for grocery and mass merchants and higher (roughly 8-15%) for specialty and off-price leaders. The spread is driven by gross margin mix (private label, apparel), inventory discipline, and store productivity.

key_metrics.name: Same-store sales (comps)
key_metrics.what: Growth in sales at stores open at least a year, separating organic health from new-store openings.

key_metrics.name: Sales per square foot
key_metrics.what: Store productivity, used to compare formats and decide on closures or remodels.

key_metrics.name: Inventory turnover
key_metrics.what: How many times inventory sells through per year; faster turns free cash and cut markdowns.

key_metrics.name: GMROI
key_metrics.what: Gross margin dollars earned per dollar of average inventory, the merchant's core profitability lens.

key_metrics.name: Traffic, conversion, and average ticket
key_metrics.what: Decomposes store sales into visits, share of visits that buy, and basket size.

key_metrics.name: Shrink rate
key_metrics.what: Inventory lost to theft, damage, and error as a share of sales, a current pressure point.

trends: Scale winners such as Walmart, Costco, and Amazon gaining share while mid-tier chains and department stores struggle
Retail media networks becoming a high-margin profit pool built on shopper data
Omnichannel fulfillment (buy online pick up in store, same-day delivery) using stores as mini warehouses
Off-price and value formats benefiting from cautious consumers and trade-down
Tariff and sourcing shifts pressuring import-heavy categories and prompting supply-chain diversification
Automation and AI in forecasting, pricing, and store operations to offset labor costs

case_angles.question: A national retailer's same-store sales are declining; diagnose the drivers and recommend a plan.
Should a grocery chain launch its own retail media network?
A department store chain needs to decide which stores to close.
How should a big-box retailer respond to Amazon expanding same-day delivery in its markets?

interview_hooks: Is the physical store a cost center or a strategic asset in an omnichannel world?
Will retail media meaningfully change retailer economics, or is it a reclassification of trade funds?
Can mid-sized retailers survive without the scale of Walmart, Costco, and Amazon?
